chunks: Salih al-Qammat narrated to us, from Aban ibn Taghlub, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

'The people are four (types).' So I said, 'May I be your ransom! And what are they?' So he said: 'A man given iman (faith) but not given the Quran; and a man given the Quran but not given iman; and a man given the Quran and given iman; and a man not given the Quran nor iman.'

He said: I said, 'May I be your ransom! Explain their states to me.' So he said: 'As for the one given iman but not given the Quran, his example is like the example of the date — its taste is sweet, but there is no aroma for it. And as for the one given the Quran but not given iman, his example is like the example of the myrtle — its aroma is pleasant but its taste is bitter. And as for the one given the Quran and iman, his example is like the example of the citron (utruja) — its aroma is pleasant and its taste is good. And as for the one not given iman nor the Quran, his example is like the example of the colocynth — its taste is bitter and there is no aroma for it.'

key_terms.الأترجة: Utruja/Citron — a citrus fruit prized in classical Arabic culture for its simultaneous fragrance and sweet taste; frequently used as an ideal metaphor in hadith
key_terms.الإيمان: Iman — inner, heartfelt faith; belief and conviction in the fundamentals of religion
key_terms.الحنظلة: Colocynth — an extremely bitter wild gourd; symbol of something wholly devoid of goodness
key_terms.القرآن: The Quran — here refers both to its text and to embodying its guidance; receiving (إيتاء) the Quran implies truly benefiting from it
key_terms.جعلت فداك: May I be your ransom/sacrifice — a reverential formula used by companions when addressing the Imams (AS)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic teaching about having Quran and iman according to Imam Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) presents a memorable typology of people based on whether they have been granted iman (inner faith) and knowledge of the Quran. Using four fruits as parables — the date (sweet but odorless), the myrtle (fragrant but bitter), the citron (fragrant and sweet), and the colocynth (bitter and odorless) — the Imam illustrates that mere recitation or memorization of the Quran without true faith is incomplete, while genuine faith without Quranic knowledge also lacks a dimension of beauty. The ideal is the person blessed with both, like the citron, whose outward presentation and inner substance are both excellent. This teaching was addressed to Aban ibn Taghlub, himself a celebrated Quran reciter and jurist, giving the parable added resonance.
